texts: mixed: every piece of content is present, but "are THE deposits" is recorded only as "silken threads are a kind of deposit" - the identity claim (these and nothing else are what nightmoths leave) has no carrier - and the relative clause has to be lifted out into a separate standing claim about nightmoths anyway. Writing the two halves as two sentences lands the same content on shapes that are fully covered: "Silken threads are deposits. Nightmoths leave silken threads on lantern rims." The exhaustive force of "the" is lost either way, so splitting gives nothing up.

good. all three properties are recorded of the kind at the usual generic strength, "slightly" is kept as a recorded degree on stickiness rather than dropped, and the threads keep both their thread genus and their silken property.

mixed: the scraping, the warm stone the threads come off, and the flat blade as the tool are all recorded correctly, but "A Keeper" mints one anonymous keeper, so this reads as one person's action rather than as what Keepers do - no rule reaches any other Keeper. A bare plural is what marks a standing practice: "Keepers scrape the threads off the warm stone with a flat blade."

mixed: the parse was reviewed and accepted, and the yield, the small heap of threads, the nightly recurrence and moth-season are all recorded - but "A well-attended lantern" mints one anonymous lantern, so a habit you mean of every well-attended lantern is stored as the habit of that single one. Use the bare plural: "Well-attended lanterns yield a small heap of threads each night in moth-season."
